description: Team from Singapore competing in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge! We combine machine learning, data visualization, and space science to analyze NASA microgravity combustion experiments. Our goal is to extract actionable fire safety insights for spacecraft cabins and future extraterrestrial habitats. Excited to innovate for mission resilience and astronaut safety!
summary: We built a web dashboard that shows what NASA knows about fire for the place a crew will live, and what it has not tested yet. It brings together NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data: 1,711 microgravity fire tests from 24 investigations, plus reports and spreadsheets we read to recover missing test conditions. Pick a place (a Moon base, the ISS, a spacesuit or Earth) to see which tests ran in its air, the nearest ones outside it, whether flames went out, and what is missing. For a Moon base, only 20 tests apply, all gas flames, and NASA’s own planned Moon atmosphere has none. No solid material in the tables was burned above 22.7% oxygen. In the Simulation, users load an example spacecraft or their own floor plan, see how much NASA evidence covers each object, and get cited guidance on detecting, stopping and preventing a fire. Every number links to its NASA source and DOI.
details:
What it does

Fire is one of the most dangerous things that can happen in a closed cabin, and future Moon and Mars habitats won’t use the same air as the ISS. A Moon base is expected to run at 30% oxygen or more and 10.2 psi or less, and NASA’s planned exploration atmosphere is 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia. Richer, thinner air changes how materials burn. NASA has run more than 1,700 microgravity fire tests, but the results are spread across 24 investigations, 22 tables, reports and raw files.

Our dashboard answers one question for mission designers, researchers and students: for the air a crew will breathe, which NASA fire tests apply, what has not been tested yet, and how should a crew detect, stop and prevent a fire there?

  • Places. Choose a place:
    Each place shows:
    Spacecraft cabin and Mars habitat are listed as “waiting”, because NASA has no current published air values for them.
    • Moon base and pressurized rover (the challenge’s range);
    • a Moon base in NASA’s exploration atmosphere;
    • the ISS;
    • a spacesuit;
    • Earth at sea level.
    • how many NASA tests ran in its air, and from which investigations and fuel types;
    • the nearest tests outside that air;
    • how flames ended there (“will it go out?”);
    • whether the gravity matches.
    • the 5 nearest real NASA tests and what they did;
    • Detection, Suppression and Prevention answers, every line cited to NASA’s tests.
    • its objectives and approach;
    • its fuels (shape and size);
    • which conditions varied between its tests;
    • what NASA measured (sensors, cited to report pages or sensor-log columns);
    • its hardware, its papers and a DOI link;
    • every test row, with its source.
    • our example spacecraft (flight deck, crew cabin and node, with a vent duct and a closed door);
    • your own 3D layout file (rooms, doors, a vent duct and objects);
    • a floor-plan picture, which AI reads into 3D. You still pick every material from NASA’s tested list.
  • Earth benefits. NASA fire-safety spinoffs already used on Earth.
  • Download. A CSV of every test, each row with its NASA table, row number and DOI, ready for anyone building flammability models.

How it works

  • The data: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), Combustion Science: 24 investigations and 22 experiment tables, 2,009 source rows. Every row is accounted for: 1,753 test rows (1,711 distinct tests, because NASA’s tables repeat 42 rows word for word), 247 rows kept in summary tables, and 9 left out with a stated reason.
    • Python scripts download PSI’s records and tables, convert them to small data files the app reads, and stop if any check fails.
    • 105 independent checks re-read NASA’s own files on every build: totals, ranges, place counts, every quote on its page, every value recovered from a spreadsheet.
    • The web app computes every count with the same shared functions, so two screens can never disagree.
    • Google Gemini reviews uploaded experiments using only numbered facts worked out by our code; any line that cites nothing real is dropped.
    • Gemini also reads a floor-plan picture into 3D, but never decides what anything is made of. Any material it returns is dropped, and an answer with any problem is refused whole.
    • Both features run through server functions, so API keys stay on the server, never in the browser or the code. Calls are limited to our own site, size-checked and capped per visitor.

What the data shows:

  • For a Moon base, only 20 NASA tests ran in its air, all gas flames from one investigation (ACME CFI-G).
  • In NASA’s own planned exploration atmosphere (34% oxygen, 8.2 psia), the tables hold no tests.
  • No solid material in PSI’s tables was burned at 30% oxygen or more; the highest is 22.7% (BASS).

Benefits

  • Mission and habitat designers: see in minutes which NASA fire tests apply to a cabin’s air, and which materials in a layout have no evidence there, before choosing materials or fire-safety equipment.
  • Safety planners: for any cabin layout and air, a cited starting point for detection, suppression and prevention, based on what NASA actually tested.
  • Researchers: a cited view of what’s been tested and what hasn’t, a ranking of under-studied investigations, and a CSV ready for flammability modelling. Each row traces back to NASA’s table and DOI.
  • Labs and future missions: new results can be added and compared with NASA’s evidence right away, without waiting for a new release of the dashboard.
  • Students and teachers: an open, visual way into NASA’s microgravity combustion data, with every number linked to its source.
  • NASA’s data itself: we found and documented problems in the source data, which can help make PSI more reliable for everyone.

Intended impact

Our aim is that no one designs a crew habitat assuming NASA has tested something it hasn’t. By showing the gaps clearly, the dashboard points to the experiments that matter most next:

  • solid materials in oxygen-rich, low-pressure air, like NASA’s planned Moon atmosphere, where PSI’s tables hold no tests;
  • partial gravity, once data from upcoming experiments (LUCI, FM2) is published.

New experiments can be compared straight away by uploading them. Once NASA publishes them in PSI, re-running our checked scripts makes them part of NASA’s own counts. The same evidence-first approach can help anyone working on fire safety where oxygen is high, in space or on Earth.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: TypeScript and JavaScript (web app and server functions), Python (data pipeline, standard library only), HTML and CSS.
  • Software and libraries: React, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber, zustand, Vercel (hosting and server functions), Google Gemini (AI features), Git and GitHub. Claude (Anthropic) helped write much of the code.
  • Hardware: none. It runs in any modern web browser and was built on our own laptops.

How it’s creative

Most fire-safety summaries list experiments. We turn them around: start from the place a crew will live and show NASA’s evidence for that air, including its gaps, on one cited dashboard, down to each object in a cabin.

  • The Simulation’s evidence map lets an engineer see, object by object, where a cabin design rests on real NASA tests and where it doesn’t. It works on our example spacecraft, their own layout, or a picture of their floor plan, and turns that into a plan for detection, suppression and prevention.
  • We went past the summary tables into NASA’s raw spreadsheets and reports, recovering conditions for 121 tests and finding problems in the source data.
  • The illustrations (the flame and the spread) show how an honest drawing can sit next to real evidence without being mistaken for it.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: real NASA data only. Missing values stay empty and are never estimated. We say “not in NASA’s tables” rather than “never tested”, because NASA’s reports may hold more. For example, NASA’s later Saffire burns aren’t in PSI.
  • Traceability: every number links to its NASA table row or report page and its DOI, as PSI asks.
  • Comparing like with like: “inverse” flames, whose oxygen comes from the burner, are kept apart from cabin-air tests, and repeated rows are counted once.
  • Gravity: every PSI test ran in microgravity, so each place says whether its gravity matches, and nothing claims to show how fire behaves on the Moon or Mars.
  • Illustration versus evidence: the flame and the spread are clearly labelled as drawings. The spread counts steps instead of time, and never changes the evidence or the guidance.
  • Keeping NASA’s evidence separate: uploaded data is useful, but it isn’t NASA’s. So it’s always marked, kept apart from NASA’s counts, and compared with NASA’s tests rather than mixed into them.
  • Responsible AI: AI works only from facts our code provides, must cite them, and is always labelled as AI. Keys stay on the server.
  • Privacy: uploaded experiments are saved in the user’s browser. An upload is sent to the AI for its review when it’s submitted. A floor-plan picture leaves the computer only when the user presses the button to draw it in 3D, and the button says where it goes.
  • Ease of use: plain-language explanations for non-specialists, filters kept in the page address so a view can be shared, and every illustration labelled.

Limitations we state openly:

  • Every PSI test ran in microgravity.
  • Many tests lack a recorded pressure and can’t be placed.
  • The tables are summaries, and reports may hold more.
  • The illustrations are drawings, not models.
